all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: virtual tour
concepts.definition: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

defining_facts.text: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.

Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: node
concepts.definition: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

defining_facts.text: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.
In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.
For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

concepts.name: empirical study
concepts.definition: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

defining_facts.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.
The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.

An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.

concepts.name: natural walking model
concepts.definition: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

defining_facts.text: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.
The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.
The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

concepts.name: travel time
concepts.definition: The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

defining_facts.text: The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

concepts.name: vertex set
concepts.definition: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

defining_facts.text: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

concepts.name: edge weight
concepts.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

defining_facts.text: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

For a path P in a graph that contains n vertices, the total travel time for P is the sum over i = 1 to n - 1 of the edge weight epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive vertices, and epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices.

For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

concepts.name: complete graph
concepts.definition: The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.

defining_facts.text: The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.

After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances.

The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.
The first stage of the algorithm is to compute the complete graph G dash by replacing every pair of vertices that is not directly connected with the shortest path between those vertices.

The algorithm then replaces the edge weights in the complete graph, which are originally the Euclidean distances between node pairs, with travel times t computed using the natural walking model, producing the final graph G double dash, whose edges are weighted by travel duration to give a realistic experience.

concepts.name: shortest path
concepts.definition: The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks, given a complete graph, for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.

defining_facts.text: The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks, given a complete graph, for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.

For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

never_defined.name: virtual environment
never_defined.definition: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

never_defined.name: path
never_defined.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

never_defined.name: route
never_defined.definition: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

never_defined.name: vertex

never_defined.name: euclidean distance
never_defined.definition: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

never_defined.name: edge set
never_defined.definition: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

never_defined.name: movement time
never_defined.definition: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

never_defined.name: experience time
never_defined.definition: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

never_defined.name: virtual reality exposure time
never_defined.definition: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

never_defined.name: virtual world graph
never_defined.definition: A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness (CS) if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

never_defined.name: traversal time
never_defined.definition: A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness (CS) if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

never_defined.name: movement speed
never_defined.definition: There is no easy way to determine the time threshold (TTH); recommended thresholds may depend on content and movement speed, and a threshold can be obtained from an empirical study with a limited number of users or from pre-existing study results.

never_defined.name: tour
never_defined.definition: When planning a tour to be completed within a given time threshold, visiting every node or vertex representing a point of interest is neither mandatory nor always possible.

never_defined.name: total completion time
never_defined.definition: The revised virtual reality path optimization problem maximizes the total importance F(P) of a path P subject to the constraint that the path's total completion time, T(P) + W(P), is less than or equal to the time threshold T_H.

never_defined.name: vehicle routing problem
never_defined.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

never_defined.name: operations research problem
never_defined.definition: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

never_defined.name: fully connected graph
never_defined.definition: The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.

never_defined.name: importance value
never_defined.definition: The desired output of the algorithm is the optimal path P that maximizes the importance value F, covers the maximum number of most important points of interest (POIs), and keeps the total exposure time, i.e. the traveling time plus the waiting time, less than the time threshold.

never_defined.name: virtual reality path planning solver
never_defined.definition: The final graph G double dash, together with the importance f and waiting time w of each node, is given as input to a virtual reality path planning (VRPP) solver, and the solver returns the optimal path P_opt.

never_defined.name: modified optimal path
never_defined.definition: The optimal path returned by the solver is modified by replacing each hypothetical edge between vertices V_i and V_j with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph, and the algorithm returns this modified optimal path.
